table.caption: Yeast cells per milliliter in a flask of sugar solution, counted every 2 hours (invented data for practice)

items.q: During which period does the yeast population double every 2 hours?
options: From 0 to 6 hours
From 8 to 12 hours
From 12 to 16 hours
Over the whole 16 hours

why.correct: Steady doubling is the sign of exponential growth.
options: Right: 10, 20, 40, 80 thousand cells per mL, doubling each 2 hours.
From 150 to 240 to 300, growth is slowing, not doubling.
The population is leveling off: 300, 320, 325.
Doubling stops after about 6 hours.

items.q: Which statement best describes the shape of the whole yeast growth curve?
options: A J-curve that rises faster and faster to the end
An S-curve leveling off near 325 thousand cells per mL
A straight line rising at a steady rate
A curve that rises and then crashes to zero

why.correct: Rapid growth that slows and levels off is logistic.
options: After 8 hours growth slows, so it is not a J-curve throughout.
Right: fast early growth, then slowing, then a plateau: logistic growth.
Growth is not steady: it speeds up, then slows.
The population levels off; it does not crash in these 16 hours.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the yeast population leveling off after 12 hours?
options: The yeast cells stop dividing once they are 12 hours old
The flask gets colder each hour of the experiment
Sugar runs low and wastes build up
Yeast stop growing at a set 300 thousand cells per mL

why.correct: A population levels off when limiting factors strengthen as it grows.
options: Cells keep dividing when there is food; age is not the limit.
Nothing suggests the temperature changed.
Right: density-dependent limits (food and waste) slow growth near carrying capacity.
The level depends on the flask’s resources, not a fixed number.

items.q: How many times larger is the yeast population at 6 hours than at 0 hours?

why.correct: Divide the later count by the earlier one: $\frac{80}{10} = 8$ times. That is three doublings in 6 hours ($2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$), one every 2 hours.

mistakes.why: That is the increase (80 - 10), not how many times larger. Divide: 80 / 10.
That is the number of doublings. Each doubling multiplies by 2, so three doublings make it 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 times larger.

items.q: On the figure, at about what population size does the logistic curve grow fastest?
options: About 1,000, at the carrying capacity
About 20, at the start
About 1,400, at the top of the graph
About 500, half the carrying capacity

why.correct: Logistic growth is fastest at about half of K.
options: At K the curve is flat; growth has stopped.
At the start the curve is low and flat; few individuals means few added.
The logistic curve never reaches 1,400.
Right: the logistic curve is steepest at about K/2, marked on the figure.

items.q: Both curves start at 20 and match for the first few years. Why do they separate later?
options: Limits slow the S-curve near K
The J-curve species has a lower biotic potential
The S-curve species dies out after 15 years
The J-curve stops growing once it reaches the carrying capacity

why.correct: When a population is small, limits barely matter, so logistic growth looks exponential.
options: Right: limiting factors bend the logistic curve; the exponential curve assumes no limits.
Both start with the same growth; the J-curve is not slower.
The S-curve levels off near 1,000; it does not die out.
The J-curve passes 1,000 and keeps rising.

items.q: Which real situation is most likely to produce the J-curve in the figure for a time?
options: A deer herd that has lived on the same island for centuries
A species brought to a new region with no predators
A fish population in a small, crowded pond
A population that is hit by a hard winter each year

why.correct: Exponential growth needs plentiful resources and few limits, which a new, open habitat can provide.
options: A long-settled herd is usually near carrying capacity, not growing exponentially.
Right: unlimited resources and few limits let a population grow exponentially for a while.
Crowding means strong limits, which produce an S-curve or a decline.
Repeated losses keep a population from exponential growth.

items.q: A herd of 400 elk lives in a valley of 25 square kilometers. What is its population density?

why.correct: Number over area: $\frac{400\,\text{elk}}{25\,\text{km}^2} = 16$ elk per km².

mistakes.why: That is area over number. Population density is individuals per area: 400 / 25.
That multiplies. Density is individuals divided by area.

items.q: A population of 5,000 grows exponentially at 4% a year. By the rule of 70, how many years does it take to double? Write the setup, then the answer.

why.correct: Rule of 70: $\frac{70}{4} = 17.5$ years. The population reaches 10,000 in about 17.5 years, then 20,000 about 17.5 years after that.

mistakes.why: That divides by 0.04. Use the rate in percent: 70 / 4.
That is 4 / 70. Divide 70 by the rate.
Use the growth rate in percent (4), not as a decimal (0.04).
The rule of 70 puts 70 on top: 70 divided by the growth rate.

items.q: The population of 5,000 keeps growing at 4% a year. Using its doubling time of 17.5 years, how large will it be after 35 years?

mistakes.why: That is one doubling. 35 years is two doubling times: 5,000 × 2 × 2.
That adds 4% a year as a fixed number (200 a year). Exponential growth compounds: it doubles every 17.5 years.

options: A disease that spreads faster in crowded herds
Competition among birds for the few nesting sites
A late frost that kills plants
Predators that hunt more where prey is dense

why.correct: Density-independent factors act no matter how many individuals there are.
options: Spread through crowding makes disease density-dependent.
Competition gets stronger as density rises: density-dependent.
Right: a frost acts on the population regardless of its density.
Predation that tracks prey density is density-dependent.

items.q: Which limiting factors are density-dependent? Select all that apply.
options: Food that runs short as more animals share it
A parasite that passes easily between crowded hosts
A hurricane that floods a coastal marsh
A wildfire started by lightning

why.correct: Density-dependent factors strengthen as a population becomes denser.
options: Right: shortage grows with density.
Right: transmission rises with crowding.
A storm acts whatever the population size: density-independent.
Fire acts regardless of density: density-independent.

items.q: Explain why a population growing logistically slows down as it nears carrying capacity.

why.correct: More individuals, fewer resources each, fewer births and more deaths, slower growth.

specific.frame: As the population grows, ___, so ___, which ___.

cause.label: Change in resources
options: each individual gets a smaller share of food and space
each individual gets more food than before
the carrying capacity keeps rising

why.1: More individuals share the same resources, so each gets less.
why.2: Carrying capacity is set by resources; it does not rise because the population grows.

effect.label: Effect on individuals
options: fewer young are born and more individuals die
more young are born
no individuals die

why.1: Shortage lowers births; it does not raise them.

mechanism.label: Effect on growth
options: slows growth until the population levels off near K
speeds growth past K for good
makes the population grow exponentially

why.1: A population cannot stay above K for good.

specific.model: As the population grows, each individual gets a smaller share of food and space, so fewer young are born and more individuals die, which slows growth until the population levels off near K.

items.q: Rabbits released in Australia in 1859 multiplied into hundreds of millions within a few decades. Which conditions best explain this?
options: A small area of habitat with many predators
Strong competition from native rabbits
Frequent floods that killed most young rabbits
Plenty of food and few predators or diseases

why.correct: A new environment with few limits allows exponential growth, at least for a time.
options: Many predators and little habitat would limit growth.
Australia had no native rabbits to compete with them.
Heavy losses would slow growth, not speed it.
Right: with few limiting factors, the population grew exponentially.

items.q: A lake population of fish has leveled off at about 2,000. A factory then adds waste that kills half the fish’s food supply. What is the most likely result?
options: They fall toward a lower level
The fish begin to grow exponentially
The population stays steady at about 2,000
The fish population doubles in size

why.correct: When a limiting resource shrinks, the level a population settles at shrinks too.
options: Right: less food lowers carrying capacity, so the population falls.
Less food means stronger limits, not fewer.
The lake can no longer feed 2,000 fish.
Less food cannot support a larger population.
